chapter_title: Measurement and Interpretation of Groundwater Conditions and Hydraulic Properties of Soil and Rock

sections.title: Groundwater Concepts and Measurement Devices
sections.summary: Total hydraulic head h = ze + u/γw; Darcy's law: q = k × i × A. Anisotropy: kh/kv = 0.9–2.2 (glacial till); 2–10 (varved clay). Groundwater in monitoring wells (screened pipe; allow equilibration) or piezometers. Piezometer types: standpipe (simple), pneumatic (no water in tubes), vibrating wire (data logger). CPT in sands: u0 = hydrostatic; CPTU in clays: dissipation test needed for u0. Clean drilling (hollow stem auger, clean water) required to avoid contaminating measurements.
sections.body:
Hydraulic head: h = he + hp = ze + u/γw (ignoring velocity head). Pressure head hp = u/γw; elevation head he = ze. For no-flow condition, hydraulic head is constant with depth. Darcy's law: q = k × i × A where i = dh/dl. Valid for laminar flow conditions (Re < 1-10).

Monitoring wells: PVC or steel pipe with screened section (typically 1.5 m long) surrounded by sand pack; bentonite seal above sand pack; grout seal to surface. Allow equilibration time after drilling — time depends on k (minutes for sands; days to weeks for clays). Standpipe piezometer response time per Hvorslev (1951).

Piezometer types: (1) Standpipe — open pipe, simplest, slow response in low-k soils; good for most sands and gravels. (2) Twin-tube hydraulic — closed system, no water in tubes; good for low-k soils. (3) Pneumatic — twin-tube diaphragm; no water in lines, suitable for freezing conditions; less expensive. (4) Electrical resistance — strain gauge; rapid response; data logger compatible. (5) Vibrating wire — most common for permanent installations; automatic data logger; high accuracy and long-term reliability.

CPT/CPTU groundwater: In coarse-grained soils, measured pore pressure u2 = u0 (hydrostatic) since drainage is complete. In fine-grained soils, excess pore pressures develop during cone advance; dissipation tests required to determine u0 (initial pore pressure). Dissipation test: stop cone advance, record pore pressure decay vs. time; ch from Robertson et al. (1992) chart.

Geophysical methods: Time-domain electromagnetic (TEM), seismic refraction (Vp changes at water table), self-potential (SP) for seepage detection.
key_points: Total head: h = ze + u/γw; Darcy's law: q = k × i × A
Monitoring wells: allow equilibration time; days to weeks for low-k soils
Vibrating wire piezometers most common for permanent installations — data logger compatible
CPTU in fine-grained soils: u2 ≠ u0 during advance; dissipation test required for u0
Clean drilling required — hollow stem auger or clean water drilling fluid

sections.title: Hydraulic Conductivity Testing and Estimation
sections.summary: Field tests for hydraulic conductivity: auger hole seepage (variable head in unlined hole), slug/bail tests in standpipe piezometers (Hvorslev and Cooper-Bredehoeft analysis), packer tests in rock boreholes (constant or falling head), Guelph permeameter (constant head in hand-augered hole), pumping tests (most representative; Theis confined equation: k = Q×W(u)/(4πb) per observation well drawdown). Laboratory tests: flexible-wall permeameter (ASTM D5084, preferred for low-k soils), rigid-wall permeameter, consolidation cell. Correlations: Hazen equation k = C × D10² (C ≈ 1.0 cm/s, D10 in cm) for clean sands; Kozeny-Carman for granular soils. For clays: k decreases with increasing PI and Cc.
sections.body:
Field tests for hydraulic conductivity: (1) Auger hole seepage test — open borehole below water table; variable head; suitable for relatively permeable soils. (2) Slug/bail tests in standpipe piezometers — Hvorslev method (straight-line method on semi-log plot) and Cooper-Bredehoeft (type curve matching); kh from Bourdon equation. (3) Packer tests in rock — isolate zone with inflatable packers; apply constant head or falling head; measures krock for specific zone. (4) Guelph permeameter — constant head in hand-augered hole; quick measurement of kfs (field-saturated hydraulic conductivity). (5) Boutwell two-stage permeameter — obtains both kv and kh from same hole. (6) Pumping tests — most representative; for confined aquifer: k = Q×W(u)/(4πb) (Theis equation, Eq 10.24) where W(u) = well function.

Laboratory tests: Flexible-wall permeameter (ASTM D5084) — specimen in latex membrane under controlled effective stress; preferred for low-k soils (< 10-5 cm/s). Rigid-wall permeameter — simpler but sidewall leakage risk. Consolidation test k = cv × mv × γw calculated indirectly.

Correlations for granular soils: Hazen equation: k = C × D10² where C ≈ 0.8–1.2 cm/s (D10 in cm) for clean, uniform sands. Kozeny-Carman equation: k = f(e, gradation) — applicable for sands and gravels; NOT for clayey soils.

Correlations for fine-grained soils: k from PI, CC, and Ck (coefficient relating k to e). kh estimated from CPTU t50 (time for 50% dissipation) per empirical chart (Figure 10-37). DMT: kh from DMT DMTC dissipation test.
key_points: Pumping tests most representative for kh; Theis equation for confined aquifer interpretation
Slug tests (Hvorslev, Cooper-Bredehoeft): simple but only point estimate of kh near well screen
Flexible-wall permeameter (ASTM D5084) preferred for low-k soils
Hazen: k = C × D10² (C ≈ 1.0 cm/s, D10 in cm); clean uniform sands only
kh from CPTU t50 dissipation time — empirical chart (Figure 10-37)
